title: Field Notes on Kelp Curing in the Orrin Isles
markdown:
<!-- p:1 -->

# Chapter 1: Harvest and drying

## 1.1 Harvest tides

The kelp of the Orrin Isles is cut only during the second low tide after a full moon, when the water drops far enough to expose the deepest beds. Harvesters wade out with short bronze sickles and cut each frond a hand's width above the holdfast, so that the plant grows back within a single season.

Nets are forbidden on the beds. The islanders believe that dragging a net tears the holdfasts from the rock, and a bed torn that way takes nine years to recover. A family that is caught netting loses its right to harvest for the rest of the year.

The cut fronds are carried ashore in wicker baskets lined with wet sacking, because kelp that dries in the sun before it reaches the racks turns brittle and loses most of its sweetness.

<!-- p:2 -->

## 1.2 The Marrick drying racks

Once ashore, the fronds are hung over the Marrick racks, long frames of driftwood that always face north. Direct sunlight bleaches the kelp to a pale yellow, so the racks are turned away from the midday sun and the fronds dry only in the wind.

Drying takes exactly eleven days. On the sixth day every frond is turned by hand so that both sides are exposed to the wind. If it rains for more than two days in a row, the whole harvest is moved into the net sheds and the eleven days are counted again from the start.

A well dried frond loses four fifths of its weight: a hundred kilograms of fresh kelp give about twenty kilograms of finished product.

<!-- p:3 -->

## 1.3 Salt and smoke

After drying, the kelp is rubbed with coarse sea salt, forty grams for every kilogram of dried fronds. The salt draws out the last moisture and keeps moulds away during storage.

The salted fronds are then cold smoked for three nights over a fire of peat mixed with juniper branches. Peat alone gives a bitter taste, and the juniper softens it. The fire must never be hot enough to cook the kelp: a smoker who can hold his palm above the embers for a slow count of ten is doing it right.

<!-- p:4 -->

# Chapter 2: Grading, storage and trade

## 2.1 Tasting and grading

The best kelp, called first cut, is dark green, almost black, and snaps cleanly when bent. It smells of iodine and fresh hay. Kelp that bends without breaking still holds water and is sold as second cut, at half the price.

Graders also chew a small piece: first cut dissolves slowly and leaves a sweet aftertaste, while kelp that was bleached by the sun tastes of nothing but salt.

<!-- p:5 -->

## 2.2 Winter storage

For the winter the cured kelp is packed into sealed clay jars, which are buried in dry sand under the floor of the boathouses. The sand keeps the jars at an even temperature and away from the damp sea air.

Kept this way, the kelp holds its flavour for three winters. After the third winter it is no longer sold as food and is used instead to fertilise the potato fields.

<!-- p:6 -->

## 2.3 The guild ledgers

All sales went through the guild of Tallow Quay. Its harbour clerk kept the ledger, writing down the family, the weight and the grade of every load that left the island.

A family caught selling damp kelp as first cut was banned from the market for a whole season, and its name was written in red ink in the ledger. In the best years, a bale of first cut was worth as much as a young goat.
